begin-play: Begin Play runs once when the actor enters the world. This is the setup step, not a loop. It runs when the wire into it fires, and the wires out of it wait until it finishes. For example, a patrol arms its one-second timer here, and then the actor is free to stand still.
end-play: End Play runs when the actor is leaving. Use it to stop timers and drop what this actor owned. It runs when the wire into it fires, and the wires out of it wait until it finishes. For example, a designer uses end play when a pawn needs that step and not a frame loop.
tick: Tick runs every frame. Anything on this line repeats for as long as the actor is alive. It runs when the wire into it fires, and the wires out of it wait until it finishes. For example, writing health here would drain the player while the pause menu is open.
enhanced-input: This is the key or button press. The rest of the function runs only when that action fires. It runs when the wire into it fires, and the wires out of it wait until it finishes. For example, IA_Interact is the use key. The trace does not know which keyboard key was bound.
custom-event: This is a named event. It runs when something else calls that name. It runs when the wire into it fires, and the wires out of it wait until it finishes. For example, a designer uses custom event when a pawn needs that step and not a frame loop.
line-trace: A line trace asks the physics scene what the aim hits, and stores that hit. It runs when the wire into it fires, and the wires out of it wait until it finishes. For example, a rifle asks what the crosshair touches, once, when the player fires.
sphere-trace: A sphere trace is a thick sweep. It asks what a ball along the aim would bump. It runs when the wire into it fires, and the wires out of it wait until it finishes. For example, a designer uses sphere trace when a pawn needs that step and not a frame loop.
break-hit: Break Hit pulls the actor, the point, and the bone out of the trace result. It runs when the wire into it fires, and the wires out of it wait until it finishes. For example, a designer uses break hit when a pawn needs that step and not a frame loop.
apply-damage: Apply Damage tells the hit actor it was hurt, and names the damage type. It runs when the wire into it fires, and the wires out of it wait until it finishes. For example, a designer uses apply damage when a pawn needs that step and not a frame loop.
destroy-actor: Destroy removes that actor from the world. It runs when the wire into it fires, and the wires out of it wait until it finishes. For example, a designer uses destroy actor when a pawn needs that step and not a frame loop.
play-sound: Play Sound starts a sound at a point in the world. It runs when the wire into it fires, and the wires out of it wait until it finishes. For example, a designer uses play sound when a pawn needs that step and not a frame loop.
spawn-niagara: Spawn Niagara starts a particle system at a point in the world. It runs when the wire into it fires, and the wires out of it wait until it finishes. For example, a designer uses spawn niagara when a pawn needs that step and not a frame loop.
set-blackboard: Set Blackboard writes one value the AI can read later. It runs when the wire into it fires, and the wires out of it wait until it finishes. For example, a designer uses set blackboard when a pawn needs that step and not a frame loop.
move-to: Move To asks the AI controller to walk toward a point. It runs when the wire into it fires, and the wires out of it wait until it finishes. For example, a designer uses move to when a pawn needs that step and not a frame loop.
activate-ability-tag: This tries to start the ability that carries that gameplay tag. It runs when the wire into it fires, and the wires out of it wait until it finishes. For example, a designer uses activate ability tag when a pawn needs that step and not a frame loop.
activate-ability-class: This tries to start one ability class on this actor. It runs when the wire into it fires, and the wires out of it wait until it finishes. For example, a designer uses activate ability class when a pawn needs that step and not a frame loop.
apply-effect-self: This applies a gameplay effect to the same actor, such as a buff or a cost. It runs when the wire into it fires, and the wires out of it wait until it finishes. For example, a designer uses apply effect self when a pawn needs that step and not a frame loop.
has-gameplay-tag: This asks whether the actor currently has that gameplay tag. It runs when the wire into it fires, and the wires out of it wait until it finishes. For example, a designer uses has gameplay tag when a pawn needs that step and not a frame loop.
get-player-character: This gets the character the local player is controlling. It runs when the wire into it fires, and the wires out of it wait until it finishes. For example, a designer uses get player character when a pawn needs that step and not a frame loop.
get-player-controller: This gets the player controller, the object that owns input for that player. It runs when the wire into it fires, and the wires out of it wait until it finishes. For example, a designer uses get player controller when a pawn needs that step and not a frame loop.
switch-authority: This splits the graph. The authority side is the server. The other side is everyone else. It runs when the wire into it fires, and the wires out of it wait until it finishes. For example, a designer uses switch authority when a pawn needs that step and not a frame loop.
has-authority: This asks if this machine is the authority. Shared numbers should change only when the answer is yes. It runs when the wire into it fires, and the wires out of it wait until it finishes. For example, only the listen server should subtract the shared health float.
branch: Branch is an if. One pin runs when the condition is true, the other when it is false. It runs when the wire into it fires, and the wires out of it wait until it finishes. For example, a reload branch stops you when the magazine is already full.
sequence: Sequence runs the following pins in order, one after another. It runs when the wire into it fires, and the wires out of it wait until it finishes. For example, a designer uses sequence when a pawn needs that step and not a frame loop.
forloop: For Loop counts from the first index to the last and runs the body each time. It runs when the wire into it fires, and the wires out of it wait until it finishes. For example, a designer uses forloop when a pawn needs that step and not a frame loop.
foreach: For Each walks a list and runs the body once per item. It runs when the wire into it fires, and the wires out of it wait until it finishes. For example, a designer uses foreach when a pawn needs that step and not a frame loop.
while: While keeps running the body until its condition becomes false. It runs when the wire into it fires, and the wires out of it wait until it finishes. For example, a designer uses while when a pawn needs that step and not a frame loop.
print-string: Print String writes a message on the screen. It is a trace of what happened, not gameplay. It runs when the wire into it fires, and the wires out of it wait until it finishes. For example, a designer uses print string when a pawn needs that step and not a frame loop.
set-variable: Set stores a value on the component so a later step can read it. It runs when the wire into it fires, and the wires out of it wait until it finishes. For example, Set Magazine adds the rounds that fit. The number stays on the component for the HUD to read.
get-variable: Get reads a value that an earlier Set stored. It runs when the wire into it fires, and the wires out of it wait until it finishes. For example, a designer uses get variable when a pawn needs that step and not a frame loop.
literal: This is a fixed number or name typed on the node. It does not change on its own. It runs when the wire into it fires, and the wires out of it wait until it finishes. For example, a designer uses literal when a pawn needs that step and not a frame loop.
add: Add sums the two inputs. It runs when the wire into it fires, and the wires out of it wait until it finishes. For example, a designer uses add when a pawn needs that step and not a frame loop.
subtract: Subtract takes the second input off the first. It runs when the wire into it fires, and the wires out of it wait until it finishes. For example, a designer uses subtract when a pawn needs that step and not a frame loop.
multiply: Multiply scales one number by the other. It runs when the wire into it fires, and the wires out of it wait until it finishes. For example, a designer uses multiply when a pawn needs that step and not a frame loop.
divide: Divide splits the first number by the second. It runs when the wire into it fires, and the wires out of it wait until it finishes. For example, a designer uses divide when a pawn needs that step and not a frame loop.
clamp: Clamp keeps a number inside a lowest and highest value. It runs when the wire into it fires, and the wires out of it wait until it finishes. For example, a limb hit is clamped so a normal shot cannot drop that limb below ten percent.
lerp: Lerp blends from the first value toward the second by the alpha. It runs when the wire into it fires, and the wires out of it wait until it finishes. For example, a designer uses lerp when a pawn needs that step and not a frame loop.
equal: Equal asks whether the two inputs are the same. It runs when the wire into it fires, and the wires out of it wait until it finishes. For example, a designer uses equal when a pawn needs that step and not a frame loop.
greater: Greater asks whether the first number is larger. It runs when the wire into it fires, and the wires out of it wait until it finishes. For example, a designer uses greater when a pawn needs that step and not a frame loop.
less: Less asks whether the first number is smaller. It runs when the wire into it fires, and the wires out of it wait until it finishes. For example, a designer uses less when a pawn needs that step and not a frame loop.
and: AND is true only when both inputs are true. It runs when the wire into it fires, and the wires out of it wait until it finishes. For example, a designer uses and when a pawn needs that step and not a frame loop.
or: OR is true when either input is true. It runs when the wire into it fires, and the wires out of it wait until it finishes. For example, a designer uses or when a pawn needs that step and not a frame loop.
not: NOT flips a yes into a no, or a no into a yes. It runs when the wire into it fires, and the wires out of it wait until it finishes. For example, a designer uses not when a pawn needs that step and not a frame loop.
select: Select picks the first value when the condition is true, and the second when it is false. It runs when the wire into it fires, and the wires out of it wait until it finishes. For example, a designer uses select when a pawn needs that step and not a frame loop.
do-once: Do Once lets the body run a single time, then stays closed. It runs when the wire into it fires, and the wires out of it wait until it finishes. For example, a designer uses do once when a pawn needs that step and not a frame loop.
gate: Gate holds the exec until something opens it. It runs when the wire into it fires, and the wires out of it wait until it finishes. For example, a designer uses gate when a pawn needs that step and not a frame loop.
flipflop: FlipFlop alternates. Each call takes the other exit. It runs when the wire into it fires, and the wires out of it wait until it finishes. For example, a designer uses flipflop when a pawn needs that step and not a frame loop.
delay: Delay waits, then continues. The actor can do other work during the wait. It runs when the wire into it fires, and the wires out of it wait until it finishes. For example, a designer uses delay when a pawn needs that step and not a frame loop.
timeline: Timeline plays a curve over time and feeds the alpha out. It runs when the wire into it fires, and the wires out of it wait until it finishes. For example, a designer uses timeline when a pawn needs that step and not a frame loop.
cast-to: Cast To checks whether the object is that class. The body runs only when the cast succeeds. It runs when the wire into it fires, and the wires out of it wait until it finishes. For example, a designer uses cast to when a pawn needs that step and not a frame loop.
dispatcher-bind: Bind connects a dispatcher to a function, so that function runs when the dispatcher fires. It runs when the wire into it fires, and the wires out of it wait until it finishes. For example, a designer uses dispatcher bind when a pawn needs that step and not a frame loop.
dispatcher-call: Call fires the dispatcher, which runs every function that bound to it. It runs when the wire into it fires, and the wires out of it wait until it finishes. For example, a designer uses dispatcher call when a pawn needs that step and not a frame loop.
make-struct: Make Struct fills in the fields of one struct value. It runs when the wire into it fires, and the wires out of it wait until it finishes. For example, a designer uses make struct when a pawn needs that step and not a frame loop.
break-struct: Break Struct pulls the fields back out of a struct. It runs when the wire into it fires, and the wires out of it wait until it finishes. For example, a designer uses break struct when a pawn needs that step and not a frame loop.
call-function: This calls another function and waits for it to return. It runs when the wire into it fires, and the wires out of it wait until it finishes. For example, a designer uses call function when a pawn needs that step and not a frame loop.
interface-call: This calls an interface. The actor that implements the interface does the work. It runs when the wire into it fires, and the wires out of it wait until it finishes. For example, Execute_Interact opens a door or grants a pickup without a cast to each Blueprint.
set-timer: Set Timer schedules a function to run later, instead of every frame. It runs when the wire into it fires, and the wires out of it wait until it finishes. For example, Sense schedules itself every fifth of a second instead of every frame.
set-timer-event: Set Timer by Event schedules an event to run later. It runs when the wire into it fires, and the wires out of it wait until it finishes. For example, a designer uses set timer event when a pawn needs that step and not a frame loop.
set-timer-function: Set Timer by Function Name schedules a function by its name. It runs when the wire into it fires, and the wires out of it wait until it finishes. For example, a designer uses set timer function when a pawn needs that step and not a frame loop.
spawn-actor: Spawn Actor creates a new actor in the world. It runs when the wire into it fires, and the wires out of it wait until it finishes. For example, a designer uses spawn actor when a pawn needs that step and not a frame loop.
any-damage: Any Damage runs when this actor is hurt. The incoming number is how much. It runs when the wire into it fires, and the wires out of it wait until it finishes. For example, a designer uses any damage when a pawn needs that step and not a frame loop.
point-damage: Point Damage runs for a hit at one spot, including where the shot landed. It runs when the wire into it fires, and the wires out of it wait until it finishes. For example, a designer uses point damage when a pawn needs that step and not a frame loop.
begin-overlap: Begin Overlap runs when another actor starts touching this one. It runs when the wire into it fires, and the wires out of it wait until it finishes. For example, walking into a medkit is the overlap. The use key is a different event.
end-overlap: End Overlap runs when the other actor stops touching this one. It runs when the wire into it fires, and the wires out of it wait until it finishes. For example, a designer uses end overlap when a pawn needs that step and not a frame loop.
hit: Hit runs when a blocking collision happens. It runs when the wire into it fires, and the wires out of it wait until it finishes. For example, a designer uses hit when a pawn needs that step and not a frame loop.
on-rep: OnRep runs on the other machines after a replicated property arrives. It runs when the wire into it fires, and the wires out of it wait until it finishes. For example, OnRep_Health plays the flinch after the server's health value arrives.
call-user: This calls a function you added on the component. It runs when the wire into it fires, and the wires out of it wait until it finishes. For example, a designer uses call user when a pawn needs that step and not a frame loop.
call-macro: This runs a macro, a reusable chain of nodes. It runs when the wire into it fires, and the wires out of it wait until it finishes. For example, a designer uses call macro when a pawn needs that step and not a frame loop.
rpc-server: A Server RPC asks the authority to run this. Clients do not apply it themselves. It runs when the wire into it fires, and the wires out of it wait until it finishes. For example, a designer uses rpc server when a pawn needs that step and not a frame loop.
rpc-client: A Client RPC runs on the owning client. It runs when the wire into it fires, and the wires out of it wait until it finishes. For example, a designer uses rpc client when a pawn needs that step and not a frame loop.
rpc-multicast: A Multicast RPC runs on the server and on the clients. It runs when the wire into it fires, and the wires out of it wait until it finishes. For example, a designer uses rpc multicast when a pawn needs that step and not a frame loop.
